message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything for tomorrow.

## Van name ideas

- **Sofa So Good**
- **Van Gogh**
- **The Chest Express**
- **Dovetail Dash**
- **Veneer Express**

## Route: **B → A → C**

B must come first. Going to A first gets him to B at 09:40 at the earliest, after it opens. And C can't be before A, because C won't accept anything until 11:00, after A's window has closed.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B. Done 25 minutes before it opens ✓ |
| 09:30 | Arrive at A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A. Within the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 10:25 | Arrive near C (40 min) |
| **10:25–10:55** | **30-minute break**, taken while waiting for C to open to deliveries |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C ✓ |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** (45 min) |

**There's no slack at the end.** He gets back at exactly 12:00. That's fixed by C: the earliest it accepts deliveries (11:00), plus 15 minutes of unloading and 45 minutes of driving. If C keeps him waiting even a few minutes, he'll be late back. Two things would help:
- **Call C today** and ask them to have someone ready at 11:00 sharp, or ask whether they could take the delivery a little earlier.
- **Check whether the 12:00 return can stretch** by 10–15 minutes if needed.

## Friendlier arrival text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three things to check before handover

1. **Condition:** no new scratches, dents or marks on the finish, checked in good light with the customer.
2. **Completeness and function:** all parts, shelves, keys and hardware are there, and the drawers and doors open and close smoothly.
3. **The right item:** it matches the order, including the piece, finish and any repairs requested.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, with a signature and photo captured on the driver's phone.** Customers can't lose an email, and you get a time-stamped record of the item's condition at handover, which settles disputes quickly. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them.

## "Proof of delivery," in one line

> A record, usually a signature and a photo, confirming that the item was delivered to the right person and place, when, and in what condition.

## Evening-before text

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Oakwood Restorations arrives tomorrow 9-10am. We'll text when the driver's on the way. Questions? Call 01234 567890

That's **145 characters** with these sample details. Long customer or business names could push it over, so check the count once your real details are in.

Two tips to keep it to a single message:
- **Use a plain hyphen and a plain apostrophe.** Typed in some apps, they turn into a dash (–) and a curly apostrophe (’), which switch the text to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit. The message would then split into several texts.
- **Avoid emoji** for the same reason.
